In #34075, the linter is complaining that:

Warning: warning: Mathlib/SetTheory/Cardinal/ContinuumHypothesis.lean:11:0: Modules starting with Mathlib.SetTheory are not allowed to import modules starting with Mathlib.Analysis. This module depends on Mathlib.Analysis.SpecificLimits.Basic
  which is imported by Mathlib.Analysis.Real.Cardinality,
  which is imported by this module. (Exceptions can be added to `overrideAllowedImportDirs`.)

I can of course add this to the list of ignores, but each time I do this I have to wait for the universe to rebuild, only to be told the next transitively dependency that needs excluding

So I guess I have two questions:

  • Should the directory dependency linter really follow transitive imports that aren't public?
  • Is my choice of filename reasonable in that PR?
Possibly this suggests that a lemma in analysis should be upstreamed instead?
Skew to the issues here, but are you aware of lake build --old (iirc)?
I believe it blindly reuses the oleans for files that have not been modified since the last build, meaning it would only rebuild the directory dependency file, but I haven't tried it yet myself.
I agree with the linter here, the continuum hypothesis file shouldn't be importing the real numbers. Everything should be written in the generality of the continuum.
Well, depending on the version of the CH: infinite subsets of the actual real numbers, or working with P(N) and injections. I do presume it works with the latter, however.
Neither! CH just tells you ℵ₁ = 𝔠.
Sure, but you want the lemmas about the other statements of it being equivalent, and they need to go somewhere
@Violeta Hernández What is the definition of 𝔠 in Mathlib? And for that matter, what's the definition of = here?
𝔠 is defined as 2 ^ ℵ₀. And the equals sign is just... the equals sign?
the definition of docs#Eq is the relation inductively given by a single constructor of type ∀ x, x = x
To answer the question that I think you're asking: there's really a continuum hypothesis ℵ₁ = 𝔠 for every universe, but they're all equivalent to the one in universe 0 (and hence, to each other)

David Michael Roberts said:

Violeta Hernández What is the definition of 𝔠 in Mathlib? And for that matter, what's the definition of = here?

To answer what I think your second question is: the type Cardinal is the quotient of the type universe by equivalences. See docs#Cardinal

Eric Wieser ha dicho:

Sure, but you want the lemmas about the other statements of it being equivalent, and they need to go somewhere

What lemmas do you want? And which of them genuinely require the real numbers, rather than just some type of cardinality continuum? (I suspect none)
@Violeta Hernández is 2 ^ ℵ₀ defined to be the set of functions from ℵ₀ to the von Neumann cardinal 2?
2 ^ ℵ₀ is defined as the cardinal of α → β for any types with #α = ℵ₀ and #β = 2
Also, = here means there is a bijection between representing sets.
docs#Cardinal.power_def
I know I'm playing devil's advocate here, but Type-mod- bijections is not how ZFC-ists define cardinals, so I'm being picky.
Though they are obviously equivalent.
It is how Lean defines cardinals, and I have some strong opinions on why that is the correct definition. But that's off-topic.

David Michael Roberts said:

Also, = here means there is a bijection between representing sets.

= is equality in the type Cardinal, which is a quotient of the type universe by type equivalences
which is mathematically equivalent to what you said, but what you said is technically speaking not the definition

Violeta Hernández said:

2 ^ ℵ₀ is defined as the cardinal of α → β for any types with #α = ℵ₀ and #β = 2

If you unfold all the definitions you get that it's definitionally equal to Cardinal.mk.{0} (ULift.{0, 0} Nat → ULift.{0, 0} (Fin 2))
Oh, I'm not saying I agree with ZFC-ists here. :-) Thanks for all the clarifications.
(I'm on record as saying Card is the large-partial-order reflection of the category of sets and injections)

I have somewhat of a hotter take regarding CH: it doesn't do very much for you mathematically. I'm not aware of any interesting results that you can prove with CH that aren't just more general theorems about ℵ₁ or 𝔠. GCH does simplify cardinal exponentiation quite a bit, but that's it, really.
e.g. the main theorem proven in #34075 is really just a theorem about minimal well-orders in an infinite type: #37965

The natural sets giving cardinals you get in eg Cichoń's diagram are definitely more interesting. one of them, the bounding number 𝔟, appears in a theorem about products of CW complexes by Brooke-Taylor. That would be a good theorem to formalise
But this is getting off-topic, sorry

Violeta Hernández said:

e.g. the main theorem proven in #34075 is really just a theorem about minimal well-orders in an infinite type: #37965

Thanks for this, indeed refactoring that lemma first makes things simpler.
